paras: The hanging of a Black man at Mer Rouge, Louisiana, was reported in September 1903, when a state news column said that a man it called a "bad negro who tried to run the town" had been "strung up to a limb" there. The single report gave no name, date, or account of who hanged him, and it did not say whether he died.

The item, printed on September 18, 1903, consisted of one sentence: "A bad negro who tried to run the town was strung up to a limb at Mer Rouge." It named no crime; the only reason it offered for the hanging was that the man had "tried to run the town." The sentence was written in the passive voice, so it identified neither the people who hanged him nor their number, and it mentioned no officers, arrest, or legal proceeding.
No report of an inquest, arrest, or prosecution appears in the coverage, and no later account confirmed whether the man survived.

The only known report ran in The Southern Sentinel's "Louisiana News Notes," a column of brief state items headed "Important News Throughout the State." There the hanging sat between a note on a drowning in the Ouachita river and a line reporting that Joe Comeaux "was hung in Cameron parish for the murder of a family," with no comment or headline of its own. The column called the victim a "bad negro" and gave his offense as trying "to run the town," without attributing that description to any source."
No other white paper and no Black newspaper in the collections is known to have carried the story, so the episode survives only as this single line.
